title: Lagrange points and forbidden regions
summary: Five places where a small body can sit still beside two big ones, which of them are stable, and the energy walls that fence an orbit in.

steps.title: Five balance points
steps.text:
In a frame turning with the Earth and the Moon, there are five points where gravity and the centrifugal force cancel: L1 between them, L2 beyond the Moon, L3 beyond the Earth, and L4 and L5 at the corners of equilateral triangles.

This preset orbits L1. Open the Analyze ▸ Modes tab (linearized about L1): two of its modes make a saddle, one growing and one decaying, so a body at L1 drifts away exponentially. Run it for three of its periods and watch the orbit unravel during the second loop.

check.success: L1, L2, and L3 are all saddles: spacecraft parked there must keep correcting.

steps.title: The forbidden region
steps.text:
The Jacobi constant C = 2Ω − v² is conserved, so the body can only be where 2Ω ≥ C. The Trajectory tab shades the forbidden region. The more energy, the lower C and the smaller that region.

Slow the body down: set ẏ₀ to 0.03 and run. C rises above its value at L1 (3.188, in the Summary), and the forbidden region closes the neck at L1: the body can no longer pass between the Earth and the Moon.

check.success: The neck is closed: with this little energy the body is trapped on the Earth's side.

steps.title: L4 is stable
steps.text: Now L4, 60° ahead of the Moon. Load the tadpole orbit and look at the Analyze ▸ Modes tab: every mode is an oscillation, so a body nudged away from L4 swings around it instead of leaving. Run it: the path traces a tadpole shape around L4.

check.success: Stable: Jupiter's Trojan asteroids have gathered at its L4 and L5 for billions of years.

steps.title: Unless the second body is too heavy
steps.text: L4 is only stable when the smaller primary has less than 3.85 % of the total mass (Routh's criterion). The Moon has 1.2 %. Choose Custom primaries with a mass ratio of 0.05 and check the Analyze ▸ Modes tab again.

check.success: Now a mode grows while it oscillates: L4 has become unstable.

steps.title: The Arenstorf orbit
steps.text: Richard Arenstorf found this periodic orbit in 1963, while working on Apollo trajectories: a spacecraft that loops around the Earth and the Moon and returns exactly to its start. Run it and check the Return error in the Summary.

check.success: Back where it started, to better than a millionth: a free return.
